content.text: {"relation":"DIVERGENT","consensus_summary":"All three blind responses converge on a Christocentric core: 'the truth' is God's self-revelation supremely personified in Jesus Christ (John 14:6; 1:14,17), with complementary secondary referents — Scripture/God's word, the gospel and apostolic doctrine, the Spirit of truth, God's covenant faithfulness (emet), and moral integrity. The consensus center is that Jesus does not merely teach the truth but IS the truth, and knowing it liberates and sanctifies.","book_summary":"The book identifies 'the truth' as God's law — the standard by which things are measured — citing Psalm 119:142 ('thy law is the truth') and 2 John 4. It explicitly flags the common teaching (Christ Himself, and God's word/the gospel that sets free) as the view it departs from.","consensus_core_identification":"The truth = God's revelation embodied personally in Jesus Christ (with word, gospel, Spirit, and divine faithfulness as integrated secondary layers).","book_core_identification":"The truth = God's law, functioning as the standard.","core_relation":"CONTRADICTS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book retains cases where 'truth' denotes God's written word (e.g., Ps 119:142; walking in the truth, 2 John 4), but excludes or reinterprets the dominant Johannine cases where truth is Christ's own person (John 14:6) and the gospel message that liberates (John 8:32; Col 1:5). Under the book's reading, texts like 'the truth shall set you free' would refer to the law as standard rather than the gospel — a reclassification of the consensus's central proof texts.","material_contradiction":"The book's own common-view note sets its identification against the consensus: the consensus says the truth is Christ Himself and the liberating gospel; the book says it is God's law, the standard. Law and gospel are theologically distinct and often deliberately contrasted categories (John 1:17: 'the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ'). Identifying 'the truth' as the law replaces, rather than refines, the personal-Christ referent at the center of consensus; accepting the book's core requires rejecting the consensus's central identification for the key Johannine contexts.","rationale":"Although 'Scripture/God's word' appears among consensus alternatives, the book does not merely narrow that alternative — it elevates 'God's law' to the exclusive primary identification while displacing the Christocentric center that every blind response names as the dominant referent. The book's explicit framing ('Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and God's word — the gospel that sets free') confirms it intends a different referent, not a refinement. Because the central referent is replaced (law-as-standard instead of Christ-in-person/gospel), while some extensional cases (Psalm 119; Johannine 'walking in truth') are retained, this is DIVERGENT with partial reclassification rather than REFINED.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue this is REFINED rather than DIVERGENT: the consensus itself lists 'the truth as Scripture/God's word' as a common alternative (with Ps 119:142/160 as proof texts), and 'God's law' could be read as a narrowing within that recognized category rather than a replacement of the consensus referent. On that view the book simply selects and sharpens an already-acknowledged layer.","confidence":"medium"}
